runtime has a special representation for `Int` that stores “small” signed numbers directly, while
larger numbers use a fast arbitrary-precision arithmetic library (usually
[GMP](https://gmplib.org/)). A “small number” is an integer that can be encoded with one fewer bits
than the platform's pointer size (i.e. 63 bits on 64-bit architectures and 31 bits on 32-bit
architectures).

  NumberField.discrNumberField.discr.{u_1} (K : Type u_1) [Field K] [NumberField K] : ℤThe absolute discriminant of a number field.  KType u_1 =Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → PropThe equality relation. It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

This type is special-cased by the compiler and overridden with an efficient implementation. The
runtime has a special representation for `Int` that stores “small” signed numbers directly, while
larger numbers use a fast arbitrary-precision arithmetic library (usually
[GMP](https://gmplib.org/)). A “small number” is an integer that can be encoded with one fewer bits
than the platform's pointer size (i.e. 63 bits on 64-bit architectures and 31 bits on 32-bit
architectures).

Warning: this can easily be abused. See the rest of this docstring for details.

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally,
but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system
in specific circumstances.

For example, `ZMod p` is a field if and only if `p` is a prime number.
In order to be able to find this field instance automatically by type class search,
we have to turn `p.prime` into an instance implicit assumption.

On the other hand, making `Nat.prime` a class would require a major refactoring of the library,
and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.
The compromise is to add the assumption `[Fact p.prime]` to `ZMod.field`.

In particular, this class is not intended for turning the type class system
into an automated theorem prover for first-order logic.  (SquarefreeSquarefree.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Monoid R] (r : R) : PropAn element of a monoid is squarefree if the only squares that

Warning: this can easily be abused. See the rest of this docstring for details.

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally,
but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system
in specific circumstances.

For example, `ZMod p` is a field if and only if `p` is a prime number.
In order to be able to find this field instance automatically by type class search,
we have to turn `p.prime` into an instance implicit assumption.

On the other hand, making `Nat.prime` a class would require a major refactoring of the library,
and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.
The compromise is to add the assumption `[Fact p.prime]` to `ZMod.field`.

into an automated theorem prover for first-order logic.  ¬Not (a : Prop) : Prop`Not p`, or `¬p`, is the negation of `p`. It is defined to be `p → False`,

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)

For a finite-dimensional vector space `V` over a field `k`, `Module.finrank k V` is equal to
the dimension of `V` over `k`.

For a general module `M` over a ring `R`, `Module.finrank R M` is defined to be the supremum of the
cardinalities of the `R`-linearly independent subsets of `M`, if this supremum is finite. It is
defined by convention to be `0` if this supremum is infinite. See `Module.rank` for a
cardinal-valued version where infinite rank modules have rank an infinite cardinal.

 KType u_1 =Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → PropThe equality relation. It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

  Module.finrankModule.finrank.{u_1, u_2} (R : Type u_1) (M : Type u_2) [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] : ℕThe rank of a module as a natural number.

For a finite-dimensional vector space `V` over a field `k`, `Module.finrank k V` is equal to
the dimension of `V` over `k`.

For a general module `M` over a ring `R`, `Module.finrank R M` is defined to be the supremum of the
cardinalities of the `R`-linearly independent subsets of `M`, if this supremum is finite. It is
defined by convention to be `0` if this supremum is infinite. See `Module.rank` for a
cardinal-valued version where infinite rank modules have rank an infinite cardinal.

Note that if `R` is not a field then there can exist modules `M` with `¬(Module.Finite R M)` but
`finrank R M ≠ 0`. For example `ℚ` has `finrank` equal to `1` over `ℤ`, because the nonempty
`ℤ`-linearly independent subsets of `ℚ` are precisely the nonzero singletons.  ℚRat : TypeRational numbers, implemented as a pair of integers `num / den` such that the

 KType u_1 =Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → PropThe equality relation. It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

  h1 ▸ h2

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally,
but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system
in specific circumstances.

For example, `ZMod p` is a field if and only if `p` is a prime number.
In order to be able to find this field instance automatically by type class search,
we have to turn `p.prime` into an instance implicit assumption.

On the other hand, making `Nat.prime` a class would require a major refactoring of the library,
and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.
The compromise is to add the assumption `[Fact p.prime]` to `ZMod.field`.

into an automated theorem prover for first-order logic.  (SquarefreeSquarefree.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Monoid R] (r : R) : PropAn element of a monoid is squarefree if the only squares that

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system

and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.
The compromise is to add the assumption `[Fact p.prime]` to `ZMod.field`.

It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.

A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
```
variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)

example : a = d :=
  Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
```
Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
Example:
```
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
        (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  Eq.subst h1 h2

example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
    (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
  h1 ▸ h2
```
The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)

This type is special-cased by the compiler and overridden with an efficient implementation. The
runtime has a special representation for `Int` that stores “small” signed numbers directly, while
larger numbers use a fast arbitrary-precision arithmetic library (usually
[GMP](https://gmplib.org/)). A “small number” is an integer that can be encoded with one fewer bits
than the platform's pointer size (i.e. 63 bits on 64-bit architectures and 31 bits on 32-bit
architectures).

Certain propositions should not be treated as a class globally,
but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system

and it is questionable whether making `Nat.prime` a class is desirable at all.

but sometimes it is very convenient to be able to use the type class system

Every abstract quadratic field is \mathbb{Q}-algebra-equivalent to Qsqrtd d for some squarefree integer d \ne 1, packaging the parameter normalization into a single existence statement.

QuadraticField K is the project-level property that a field over \mathbb{Q} is a quadratic extension. It is the abstract object of study; the standard model is a coordinate chart. The class wraps Algebra.IsQuadraticExtension ℚ K, so abstract statements can use [QuadraticField K] while still interoperating with mathlib's degree-two API.

The long-term Diophantine goal is a Baker--Heegner--Stark-style route toward class-number-one and related quadratic-field classification results. In the first blueprint this remains conditional on substantial future CM, ring-class field, modular-function, and finite-check input, and it depends on the distinction between formalized infrastructure and research scaffolding.
All Baker--Heegner--Stark nodes are deliberately marked future or external in this first blueprint. None should be read as a completed Lean proof.

Algebra equivalences and categorical isomorphisms are interchangeable in QuadraticFieldCat. This lets later transport statements use either the category-theoretic language or the concrete AlgEquiv API.
The planned output of the finite-check machinery is reusable certificates for class-number-one or nontrivial class-group computations, ultimately feeding concrete examples.
The route requires substantial CM and ring-class-field input. The current blueprint records this as an external mathematical dependency rather than a completed formalization.
Once the external CM and analytic inputs are available, the project should connect them to explicit finite Diophantine checks in quadratic fields.
The future real-quadratic unit pipeline should connect continued fractions and Pell solutions to explicit fundamental units.

The long-term route follows the classical Cox-style story around imaginary quadratic class-number-one fields, singular moduli, and ring class fields, sitting on top of the overall blueprint goal and reusing the imaginary Minkowski bound. This is not yet a Lean theorem in the project.
The project model \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] is Dedekind exactly in the same branch where it is already the full ring of integers: d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4.
The Dedekind-domain transport lemma is another shim candidate for eventual upstream movement once its final mathlib home is chosen; it backs the project Dedekind-domain statement.

The excluded parameters are genuinely degenerate: Qsqrtd 0 has nilpotents and Qsqrtd 1 has zero divisors. These facts justify the normalized condition d \ne 1 once squarefree integer parameters are in use, complementing the nonsquare field gate.

For squarefree d \ne 1, the discriminant of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) is d in the 1 \pmod 4 branch and 4d otherwise, combining the \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] basis discriminant and the half-integer basis discriminant with the ring-of-integers classification.
The discriminant formula transports from the standard model to an abstract quadratic field once an algebra equivalence to a standard parameter is chosen, reusing the ring-of-integers transport.
The \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2] basis has discriminant d when d = 1 + 4k.
The \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] basis has discriminant 4d. This is the basis calculation for the non-1 \pmod 4 branch.
The library includes concrete discriminant checks for the Gaussian, Eisenstein, and \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5}) examples, exercising the discriminant formula.
NumberField.discr_eq_of_algEquiv is a local upstream candidate for transporting absolute discriminants across algebra equivalences, used by the discriminant-formula transport.
A future class-group pipeline should turn the Minkowski representative theorem into finite norm searches for selected quadratic fields and families.

IsFundamentalUnit is the project predicate for a generator of the infinite part of a real quadratic unit group, modulo sign and inverse ambiguity. It abstracts the Pell-equation unit description into a predicate usable across coordinate models.
Fundamental-unit structure transports across ring equivalences, matching the project's broader transport-first architecture and aligning with the ring-equivalence shadow of the classification.

The rigidity proof begins with the generator relation: an equivalence between standard models sends the square-root generator to a pure square-root coordinate, forcing the two parameters to differ by a rational square. Squarefreeness then turns this relation into equality.
The imaginary quadratic branch has the explicit constant (2/\pi)\sqrt{|D|}, refining the generic representative bound under the Minkowski specialization.
The analogous imaginary result holds in the half-integer order for parameters k \le -2, specializing the norm-based unit criterion to the d \equiv 1 \pmod 4 branch.
For d < -1, the only units of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] are \pm 1. The proof specializes the Pell-equation unit criterion to imaginary parameters.

Any rational parameter can first be replaced by an integer parameter and then by a squarefree integer parameter, using rational-square rescaling. This is the normalization pipeline behind standard parameters.
The proof runs through half-integer normal forms: integral elements land in the correct explicit order according to the same mod-4 branch, supplying the non-1 \pmod 4 branch and the 1 \pmod 4 branch.
A future cleanup should unify the odd-prime and two-adic splitting statements using a Kronecker-symbol formulation where that abstraction is helpful.
For odd primes not dividing the parameter, splitting and inertia are controlled by the Legendre symbol.
General-purpose facts that are missing from mathlib are developed locally under QuadraticNumberFields/Mathlib/, mirroring likely upstream paths and feeding the upstream-candidate boundary.

General-purpose lemmas live first under QuadraticNumberFields/Mathlib/, are used locally, and should later move upstream to mathlib. Project-only results, such as the ring-of-integers classification and concrete examples, remain in the project. This boundary protects the public API from pretending local shims are already upstream facts.
Qsqrtd.minkowskiBound d specializes the number-field Minkowski bound to the quadratic field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), using the discriminant formula as the size input.
Every ideal class has a representative whose norm is at most the specialized Minkowski bound.
Squarefree standard parameters are unique: an algebra equivalence between Qsqrtd d₁ and Qsqrtd d₂ forces d_1 = d_2 under the normalized hypotheses.
Pell solutions multiply according to the norm multiplication law in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d].
IsPellSolution d n x y records the Pell-type equation x^2-dy^2=n. This is the bridge between coordinate arithmetic in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] and units.
The project-owned Zsqrtd model stays independent from mathlib's Zsqrtd except for the dedicated bridge file. This is project architecture, not an upstream API.

The coordinate model is a genuine quadratic field when the parameter is not a rational square. The blueprint therefore treats the nonsquare condition as the field-entry gate for Qsqrtd d, separating the quadratic-field cases from the degenerate parameters d = 0 and d = 1.
The automorphism group of a quadratic field has the expected dichotomy: the only automorphisms of Qsqrtd d (and hence of any abstract quadratic field) are the identity and conjugation.
QuadraticFieldCat bundles fields satisfying QuadraticField and organizes isomorphisms, functors, transport, and classification.

An abstract quadratic field has \mathbb{Q}-dimension two, hence is a number field. This supplies the finite-dimensional and characteristic-zero interface used by the later ring-of-integers, discriminant, and ideal-theory layers.
A field over \mathbb{Q} is quadratic if and only if it is isomorphic to one of the normalized standard models, turning the existence classification into a biconditional.

The project formalizes quadratic number fields over \mathbb{Q}. Its core workflow is to classify an abstract quadratic field, move to a standard coordinate model \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), compute there, and then transport the result back to the abstract field.
The stable splitting API packages split, inert, and ramified behavior for primes in quadratic number fields, building on the ring-of-integers classification.

Multiplying the parameter by a rational square does not change the quadratic field: Qsqrtd d is algebra-equivalent to Qsqrtd (a^2 * d) for nonzero a. This is the coordinate change used to clear denominators and normalize parameters.
The real quadratic branch has the explicit constant \tfrac12\sqrt{|D|}, refining the generic representative bound in the real case via the Minkowski specialization.
The conditional endgame should reuse the existing discriminant, splitting, ring-of-integers, units, and class-group check layers rather than duplicating coordinate arguments.
The classification also has a ring-equivalence shadow. This is useful when transporting invariants whose API is stated for ring equivalences rather than algebra equivalences.
The ring-of-integers classification is currently project-only: it is central to this repository but not presented as a finished mathlib theorem.
AlgEquiv.ringOfIntegers transports rings of integers across algebra equivalences and belongs to the general transport layer, underlying the ring-of-integers transport.
The classification packages the two branches away from 1 \pmod 4 and at 1 \pmod 4 into a single theorem.
The two explicit integer-ring models \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] and \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2] have norm-based unit criteria. These are used again in the unit-theory chapter.
After the standard-model classification, the result transports to any abstract quadratic field through the classification by squarefree parameters.
If d \equiv 1 \pmod 4, then the ring of integers is equivalent to \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2].
If d is squarefree, d \ne 1, and d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4, then the ring of integers of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d) is equivalent to \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d].

The sketch import surface collects work-in-progress modules such as Euclidean, class-group, continued-fraction, family, and research scaffolding. Nodes that use this surface should not be marked complete until the corresponding Lean modules are promoted to the stable import surface.
The \sqrt{-5} example contains concrete bounded-norm checks that exercise the imaginary Minkowski bound and the representative theorem, alongside the concrete ideal factorizations.
The \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] examples verify ideal factorizations above 2 and 3, serving as concrete tests of the ideal-primality API and the splitting classification.

For integer parameters, the preferred hypothesis package is [Fact (Squarefree d)] [Fact (d ≠ 1)]. These assumptions imply that (d : ℚ) is not a rational square, so they provide the standard way to turn Qsqrtd (d : ℚ) into a field via the nonsquare field gate.

The stable public import surface contains the completed, sorry-free library: standard models, abstract quadratic-field infrastructure, ring-of-integers and discriminant classifications, splitting results, units, and examples. It builds on the project architecture.

The standard coordinate model is \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d), implemented as Qsqrtd d := QuadraticAlgebra ℚ d 0. An element has real and square-root coordinates, and the generator satisfies \sqrt d^2 = d. This is the computational model used for trace, norm, conjugation, discriminants, and splitting calculations.
The standard models become objects of QuadraticFieldCat via QuadraticFieldCat.ofQsqrtd, and the forgetful functor to AlgCat ℚ keeps transport compatible with ordinary \mathbb{Q}-algebra maps.

A standard parameter is a squarefree integer d \ne 1 together with an algebra equivalence from the abstract field to Qsqrtd d. It records that an abstract field has been put into a normalized coordinate chart.
The Baker--Stark analytic/transcendence ingredients are also external assumptions at this stage, complementing the CM/ring-class-field input needed by the Cox-style route.

Blueprint nodes use explicit tags: complete only for existing Lean declarations, partial for scaffolds, future for planned mathematics, mathlib-candidate for upstreamable general facts, project-only for local APIs, and external-assumption for deferred mathematical input.

The coordinate API computes trace and norm directly in Qsqrtd d. The trace is 2 \operatorname{re}(x), and the norm homomorphisms are the bridge from coordinate calculations to ring-of-integers and unit arguments.
The prime 2 is handled by the expected congruences modulo 8 and modulo 4, completing the trichotomy at the even prime.
The intended lifecycle is: add a local shim, use it in the project, upstream it through a mathlib PR, then delete the local shim and migrate callers.
ZOnePlusSqrtOverTwo k is the project model of \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{1+4k})/2], the integral model used in the d \equiv 1 \pmod 4 branch and again sitting inside the standard coordinate model.
For primes p dividing d-1, the ideals (p,1-\sqrt d) and (p,1+\sqrt d) in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d] have coordinate membership criteria.
The quotient descriptions prove that both ideals are prime in the relevant concrete splitting branch.
Zsqrtd d is the project-owned model of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d], sitting inside the standard coordinate model. It is not mathlib's Zsqrtd; the bridge to mathlib's model is intentionally thin and isolated.
Those concrete ideals have quotient descriptions by \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, which supply the primality proofs.
A coordinate element x + y\sqrt d is a unit exactly when the corresponding Pell equation has norm 1 or -1. This is the coordinate counterpart of the norm-based unit criterion.
